endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Define ownership and derivative rights: who owns new datasets, trained models, or insights created using the de-identified data?

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Organizations should consider expanding permissible/prohibited uses to include rights around model outputs, local performance data, and monetization of data.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Draft and maintain well-defined contracts and service level agreements (SLAs) that specify content ownership, usage rights, quality standards, security requirements, and content provenance expectations for GAI systems.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: When partnering with a third party, or procuring a solution, this may affect the degree of solution customization that is possible, and may also require planning around intellectual property rights.

commentary.bottom_line: Four governance frameworks endorse contract terms that assign ownership of AI outputs, derivative data, locally trained models, and performance data, with endorsement strength ranging from must to may. No supplied study tests whether such terms protect organizational rights or reduce infringement exposure, and no supplied study measures how often the targeted hazard occurs.

perspectives.view: No study in this evidence map tests whether ownership and indemnification clauses change outcomes for health systems. No study documents how often unclear terms lead to lost rights or infringement claims. The recommendation rests on four endorsements that reflect expert consensus rather than measured effect, so certainty cannot be rated under GRADE conventions.

The endorsements differ in strength. The CHAI playbooks list ownership and derivative rights as a must. RUAIH guidance and NIST AI 600-1 say should, and the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide says may. NIST AI 600-1 places these terms in contracts and service level agreements for generative AI and adds content provenance. None of the sources reports data on whether the terms prevent disputes.

commentary.research_gap: No study describes current AI vendor contract terms in health care, the frequency of ownership or infringement disputes, or whether specific clauses such as indemnification or retained rights to locally trained models change dispute rates, costs, or an organization's ability to reuse its own performance data. Contract audits across health systems and case series of disputes would be a first step.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence includes Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations or the organizations that serve them. It is unknown whether safety-net systems, which may have fewer legal staff and less bargaining power with vendors, can obtain these terms at the same rate as larger systems.
